rv.q: Blistering? Yeah. Vulgar? Certainly. And viciously entertaining.
Those names – along with Constance Wu, Tramell Tillman and Michael Oberholtzer – can’t help but raise expectations that, frustratingly, go largely unmet.
What a waste of theater’s tools; what a sour, narrow use to put them to.
O’Hara has introduced modern life into an ever-popular genre of American theater: the booze-infused tell-all.
While Shit. Meet. Fan. isn’t all that persuasive, it delivers jolts of spiky humor and a cast of hardworking household names.
To me, the play doesn’t make the case this group of people would say that word over and over again, so unchallenged by their own members (even as Logan notes their ease at saying it at all).
It’s an interesting and worthwhile experiment but it isn’t completely successful here.
But what it lacks in genuine wit – many of O’Hara’s zingers land flat — this s–t show compensates with sheer outrageousness as the phone calls quickly turn X-rated.
All-star cast including Neil Patrick Harris, Jane Krakowski and Debra Messing can’t quite ignite a new play by Robert O’Hara that lacks destructive energy

Fan.: Satire and Secrets on the Rocks By Melissa Rose Bernardo ★★★☆☆ Seven disagreeable friends offend and overshare in Robert O’Hara’s New York–set satire If Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? taught us anything, it’s that party games and married couples are a dangerous combination—especially when alcohol is...
What might have been a searing examination of privilege and hypocrisy instead feels like an exhausting exercise in endurance.
Not funny enough for straight-up comedy, populated with characters too thin for drama, and lacking a wicked sense of caricature, it struggles to find a consistent, coherent voice.
Those intentions are clear but he does not successfully skewer his subjects.
The actors work together seamlessly to make some fundamentally unlikable characters entertaining enough to tolerate for a few hours, waiting for their well-deserved uppance to come.
Shit. Meet. Fan. keeps us engaged and entertained, laughing in our own discomfort, but bewildered at times by the glue that holds them together.
Unfortunately, ambition exceeds form despite a starry cast that leans into familiar tropes, including Neil Patrick Harris, Jane Krakowski, Constance Wu, and Debra Messing.
The cast may be the one reason the show is worth seeing, but that is not enough to clean up the messy plot, cheap vulgar humor, and pointless proceedings.

cn.t: O'Hara's star-studded satire on toxic masculinity and white privilege entertains with sharp performances and provocative premise, but critics find the execution uneven—more blistering and vulgar than incisive, with a contrived setup that doesn't fully deliver on its lofty aims.

vr.q: it was a damn good time
